papers.title: How to use Quality Improvement to enhance the portfolio for promotion and tenure in Academic Pulmonary, Critical Care and Sleep Medicine.
papers.abstract: Quality Improvement (QI) is a cornerstone for improving patient care and health care systems. However, QI activities are not always recognized within traditional promotion and tenure (P&T) pathways. As a result, faculty with significant QI expertise and impactful contributions may lack clear mechanisms and pathways for academic recognition, promotion, and career advancement. Identifying a clear QI P&T pathway may incentivize faculty to pursue QI as a career. Standardized approaches that translate QI activities into key conventional academic metrics and are documented across multiple domains for P&T are needed to address these gaps. The purpose of this manuscript is to provide a framework for Pulmonary, Critical Care and Sleep Medicine faculty to align QI work with traditional promotion criteria and encourage institutions to recognize the value and scope of QI in P&T considerations. This framework highlights strategies for documenting QI contributions across academic areas such as clinical care, education, research and service and supports faculty considering the value of pursuing an academic career in QI in Pulmonary, Critical Care and Sleep medicine.

papers.title: Chronobiology of Aging: Interactions Between Circadian Rhythms, Oxidative Stress, and Inflammation.
papers.abstract: Chronodisruption is increasingly recognised as a fundamental driver of biological aging rather than merely a consequence of advancing age. Although substantial evidence links circadian dysfunction with individual age-related diseases, the mechanistic integration of chronodisruption across the hallmarks of aging and its therapeutic implications remains fragmented. This review provides a comprehensive synthesis of current evidence describing how age-associated deterioration of the circadian timing system interacts with established hallmarks of aging, including genomic instability, epigenetic alterations, mitochondrial dysfunction, dysregulated nutrient sensing, impaired proteostasis, chronic inflammation, and cellular senescence. This article also incorporates how these interconnected mechanisms contribute to the development and progression of major age-related disorders, including neurodegenerative, cardiovascular, metabolic diseases, and cancer, highlighting shared molecular regulators such as BMAL1, CLOCK, PER, CRY, REV-ERBs, SIRT1, AMPK, and mTOR. Although several reviews exist that focus on individual diseases or isolated circadian mechanisms, this review integrates molecular, cellular, and translational evidence into a unified framework linking chronodisruption to systemic aging. This article discusses emerging chronotherapeutic strategies including chrono-phototherapy, chrono-nutrition, chrono-exercise, natural chrono-modulators, chrono-pharmacology, and precision geromedicine that aim to restore circadian homeostasis and improve healthy aging. Collectively, this review identifies circadian rhythm restoration as a promising systems-level therapeutic approach and outlines future directions for integrating chronobiology into precision interventions for age-related diseases.

papers.title: Glymphatic Dysfunction in Alzheimer's Disease: Mechanisms, Biomarkers, and Emerging Therapeutic Perspectives.
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive cognitive decline, with hallmark pathological features including amyloid-beta plaques, tau tangles, and neuronal loss. The glymphatic system, a recently discovered network responsible for brain waste clearance, plays a crucial role in maintaining cerebral homeostasis by facilitating the removal of neurotoxic metabolites, including amyloid-beta. Disruption of glymphatic function has emerged as a key factor in AD pathophysiology, contributing to the accumulation of toxic proteins and accelerating neurodegenerative processes. This narrative review explores the complex interplay between glymphatic dysfunction and AD. We discuss the mechanisms of the glymphatic system, emphasizing its reliance on cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and interstitial fluid flow to clear metabolic waste, and how this process is closely linked to sleep cycles. In AD, impaired glymphatic function, exacerbated by aging and sleep disturbances, accelerates the buildup of amyloid-beta and tau, driving neurodegeneration. Furthermore, sleep disturbances commonly observed in AD patients further hinder glymphatic activity, creating a vicious cycle that exacerbates cognitive decline. Emerging therapeutic approaches aimed at enhancing glymphatic function-including sleep regulation, pharmacological agents, and lifestyle interventions-are promising, but most findings remain preliminary and largely based on animal studies or early clinical observations. These strategies should therefore be considered exploratory until validated in large-scale human trials. By restoring efficient waste clearance, such interventions may offer novel avenues for slowing or preventing AD progression.

papers.title: Integrative therapies for symptom management in dementia from a palliative perspective: narrative review of systematic reviews and meta-analyses.
papers.abstract: Dementia affects over 55 million people worldwide, with behavioral and psychological symptoms (BPSD) impacting over 90% of individuals. Conventional pharmacotherapies offer limited benefits with substantial side effects. Integrative care therapies (ICT) represent a complementary approach, yet the evidence supporting their use has been largely absent from the palliative care literature. This narrative review synthesizes ICT systematic reviews and meta-analyses to bridge this gap. PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, PsycINFO, and the Cochrane Library were searched for systematic reviews and meta-analyses published between 2015 and June 2026 evaluating ICT for dementia symptom management. Seminal earlier works were also included when updated reviews were unavailable. Individual randomized controlled trials (RCTs), validation studies, and non-English publications were excluded, except selected sources cited for mechanistic, safety, regulatory, or pivotal-trial context. Cognitive stimulation achieved the highest evidence certainty, with high-certainty evidence for communication and social interaction and moderate-certainty evidence for cognition, quality of life (QOL), and challenging behaviors. Music therapy showed moderate-certainty evidence for depression improvement but not agitation. Light therapy and movement-based mind-body therapies (MBT) demonstrated benefit across the broadest range of domains-including cognition, BPSD, and sleep-though certainty remained low-to-very-low. Massage and aromatherapy showed consistent short-term benefits for agitation and depression. Acupuncture augmented conventional medication for improvement in cognition and activities of daily living (ADL). Dietary and herbal therapies contributed primarily to cognitive domains, with Ginkgo biloba showing the most robust BPSD evidence. Cannabinoids showed preliminary evidence for agitation and in severe disease. Across modalities, effects were often limited to the treatment period, early-stage disease showed the most robust benefits, and safety profiles were favorable. Only cognitive stimulation and music therapy achieved moderate or higher Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) ratings. Multiple ICT modalities show promising evidence for dementia symptom management that aligns with palliative care principles, though most evidence is of low-to-very-low certainty. Future research should prioritize pragmatic trials in hospice and palliative care settings using outcomes meaningful to this context, including comfort, caregiver experience, and healthcare utilization.

papers.title: Prevalence, Incidence, Clinical Presentation, and Treatment of Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome in Primary Care in the United Kingdom Between 1998 and 2025.
papers.abstract: Polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS) is a multisystemic disorder with a wide range of health consequences. We sought to describe temporal trends in the prevalence and incidence of PMOS and to characterize its clinical presentation, comorbidity burden, and pharmacological management in primary care in the United Kingdom (UK) between 1998 and 2025. Population-based matched cohort study using primary care records from the UK Clinical Practice Research Datalink. Females newly diagnosed with PMOS between the ages of 15 and 49 matched on age, general practice, calendar year of cohort entry, and duration of medical history to population controls without PMOS. Annual prevalence and incidence of diagnosed PMOS; baseline prevalence and incidence of cardinal PMOS features and various comorbidities; and pre- and post-cohort entry prevalence of hormonal contraceptive, anti-androgen, ovulation-inducing drug, and metformin use. The prevalence of diagnosed PMOS increased from < 0.1% in 1998 to 2.0% in 2025, with incidence rising from 0.1 to 3.6 per 1,000 person-years over the same period. Among 125,482 patients with newly diagnosed PMOS matched with an equal number of controls, patients with PMOS had higher baseline prevalence and incidence of cardinal features of PMOS, as well as diabetes, dyslipidemia, hypertension, cardiovascular and cerebrovascular disease, sleep apnea, thyroid disorders, endometriosis, uterine fibroids, chronic pain, depression, and anxiety. Use of anti-androgens, ovulation-inducing drugs, and metformin was substantially higher in patients with PMOS, especially in the year following diagnosis. PMOS is increasingly diagnosed in UK primary care and is associated with substantial multimorbidity and pharmacotherapy.

papers.title: Maternal exposure to sleep aids and risk of specific birth defects in the Birth Defects Study To Evaluate Pregnancy exposureS.
papers.abstract: Insomnia symptoms are often reported during pregnancy, prompting use of pharmacologic treatments. We explored associations between treatments used during the month before through the third month of pregnancy ("early pregnancy") and risk of birth defects using Birth Defects Study to Evaluate Pregnancy exposureS (BD-STEPS) data from 2014-2021. Pregnancies affected by birth defects ("cases") were identified from surveillance systems in seven states; liveborn infants without birth defects ("controls") were randomly selected from the same catchment areas. Mothers of cases and controls reported early pregnancy exposures via interview, including use of prescription, over-the-counter, or herbal sleep aids. For defects with ≥5 exposed cases, we used Firth's logistic regression to estimate propensity score-adjusted odds ratios (aORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs), adjusting for maternal age, race/ethnicity, education, body mass index, previous live birth, history of depression/anxiety, early pregnancy use of antipsychotics, anxiolytics, antidepressants, opioids, cigarettes, alcohol, and prenatal vitamins, occurrence of stressful events, occupation outside the home, health insurance, and site. Overall, 237 (7%) cases and 140 (8%) controls reported early pregnancy sleep aid use. We calculated aORs for 12/22 defects, which ranged from 0.52 for d-transposition of the great arteries to 1.61 for coarctation of the aorta. All CIs included the null. Results suggest sleep aids do not increase risk of most defects studied, but increased risk for coarctation of the aorta cannot be ruled out. Small numbers limited analyses. Studies examining the severity of underlying sleep disorders and impacts of specific sleep aids would be beneficial.

papers.title: Epileptiform Discharges in Seizure-Free Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder and the Role of Antiseizure Medications.
papers.abstract: To determine the frequency of epileptiform discharges (EPDs) in children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) without clinical seizures, assess autism severity using the Childhood Autism Rating Scale, Second Edition (CARS-2), and reassess the children after treatment with antiseizure medications (ASMs). A prospective cohort study. Place and Duration of the Study: Four autism centres in Duhok City, Kurdistan Region, Iraq, from August 2024 to August 2025. Fifty children with seizure-free ASD (aged 2.5-18 years) underwent clinical evaluation, electroencephalography (EEG) recording, and severity assessment using CARS-2. Children with EPDs were offered ASMs according to EEG pattern and clinical profile. EEG and CARS-2 assessments were repeated after 6 months. Data were analysed using SPSS version 31.0. Descriptive statistics were presented as means ± standard deviations for continuous variables and frequencies with percentages for categorical variables. For group comparisons, independent t-tests or Mann-Whitney U tests for small samples were used. A p-value <0.05 was considered statistically significant. EPDs were detected in 24 participants (48%). EPDs were focal in 19 cases (79.16) and generalised in 5 cases (20.83). Adherence to ASMs after 6 months was observed in 9 cases (37.5 %). All adherent participants demonstrated EEG improvement and significant reductions in total CARS-2 scores (p = 0.001). Improvements were also observed in the following domains: emotional response (p = 0.023), body use (p = 0.024), activity level (p = 0.026), visual response (p = 0.040), taste, smell and touch (p = 0.057), and general impression of ASD (p = 0.026). Adverse effects were reported in 6/15 (40%) participants whom started ASMs, primarily behavioural. EPDs are common in children with ASD, even in the absence of clinical seizures. When ASMs were used consistently, EEG improvements were observed, and ASD severity scores on the CARS-2 were reduced. Key Words: Anti-seizure medications, Autism spectrum disorder, Electroencephalography, Epileptiform discharges.

papers.title: Association Between Body Mass Index and Sleep-Related Outcomes in Patients with Cardiovascular Disease.
papers.abstract: To determine the association between body mass index (BMI) and sleep-related outcomes in patients with cardiovascular disease (CVD). A cross-sectional study. Place and Duration of the Study: Department of Family Medicine Clinic, Ankara Training and Research Hospital, Ankara, Turkiye, from November 2024 to February 2025. A total of 250 patients aged 18-65 years with CVD were included. Data regarding sociodemographic features, chronic conditions, and subjective sleep patterns of the participants were collected. Sleep quality was assessed using the NoSAS score and the Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS). Patients were categorised according to BMI. Categorical variables were assessed using chi-square analysis. To identify independent factors associated with excessive daytime sleepiness (EDS), multivariable logistic regression was used. Statistical significance was set at p <0.05. Among the patients, 19.6% (n = 49) demonstrated EDS, and 67.2% (n = 168) were classified as high risk for obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA). Age (p = 0.044), snoring (p = 0.003), and feeling fatigued upon waking (p = 0.014) were significantly related to obesity. Increasing BMI in participants was found to be linked with EDS (p = 0.012). In multivariable analysis, obesity (OR = 4.47), snoring (OR = 2.34), and abnormal sleep duration (OR = 2.63) were independently associated with EDS. The presence of EDS was higher in obese patients with CVD. A high proportion of the study population was classified as being at high risk of OSA. Snoring and feeling fatigued upon waking were more common among obese individuals. Effective management of CVD in family medicine and preventive healthcare requires close attention to obesity and sleep-related disorders. Key Words: Cardiovascular disease, Excessive daytime sleepiness, Obesity, Obstructive sleep apnoea.
papers.journal: Journal of the College of Physicians and Surgeons--Pakistan : JCPSP

papers.title: Lifestyle and contextual approaches for sexual dysfunction.
papers.abstract: Sexual dysfunction, encompassing entities like erectile dysfunction, Peyronie's disease, ejaculatory and orgasmic disorders, and female sexual dysfunction, is highly prevalent and substantially impacts quality of life. While medical and surgical treatments have significantly advanced in the last half-century, they may not address underlying causes or contextual elements that contribute to these multifactorial disorders. This perspective synthesizes evidence-based, holistic approaches to prevention and management of sexual dysfunction, emphasizing their role in preserving "Sexspan", the period of life characterized by satisfying sexual function and intimacy. We narratively review high-level evidence connecting two broad domains that support sexual wellness: (1) lifestyle pillars (diet, exercise, sleep, stress reduction) and (2) contextual domains (partner dynamics, mental health, hormonal wellness, and preventive health maintenance). We summarize disorder-specific applications of these domains and highlight emerging evidence integrating digital health, artificial intelligence, and regenerative approaches. Lifestyle and contextual factors influence endothelial health, hormonal balance, and psychological resilience, directly impacting sexual disorders. Mediterranean diet adherence, aerobic and resistance exercise, restorative sleep, and stress reduction each demonstrate measurable improvements in sexual outcomes across sexes. Partner-inclusive counseling and treatment, mental health care, hormonal assessment and optimization, and routine preventive screening further strengthen the effectiveness of treatments. Emerging digital tools, including wearables, artificial intelligence, and chatbots, offer precision monitoring and personalized intervention, while regenerative approaches remain investigational. In conclusion, holistic management of sexual dysfunction is evidence-based, broadly accessible, and synergistic with medical and surgical therapies. The integrative concept of Sexspan establishes a measurable framework for patients and sexual medicine practitioners alike.
